result:
At 4:17 every morning, the lighthouse blinked even though the bulb had been removed years ago.

Mara was the only one who noticed.

She lived in the keeper’s cottage at the edge of the cliffs, where the sea worried the rocks into smooth black stones and gulls screamed like unpaid debts. The lighthouse had been closed since the last keeper vanished, but each night its dark lantern room turned once toward the village, once toward the open water, and once toward the moon.

On the first morning, Mara assumed it was a trick of sleep.

On the seventh, she climbed the tower.

The stairs were damp with salt. Halfway up, she found a child’s red mitten tucked beneath a step. Near the top, she found a row of small wet footprints leading toward the lantern room.

The door was locked.

Mara pressed her ear against it.

Something on the other side was humming.

Not a song. Not exactly. More like the sound a person makes when trying to remember one.

She should have gone for help. Instead, she reached into her pocket and took out the brass key her mother had given her before dying.

“It opens what needs opening,” her mother had said.

The key had never fit any lock in the cottage. It slid into the lighthouse door as if it had been waiting there.

Inside, the lantern was dark. The windows were black mirrors. In the center of the room stood a boy in a yellow raincoat, dripping seawater onto the floor.

Mara knew him.

Everyone in the village knew him. His name was Elias, and he had gone missing thirty years ago, swept from the pier during a storm. His mother had kept his bedroom untouched until the day she died.

He looked exactly as he had in the old photograph: pale, solemn, and seven years old.

“You’re late,” he said.

Mara could not speak.

Elias pointed toward the sea. Far below, something glimmered beneath the waves—a long road of pale light descending into the deep.

“People keep getting lost,” he said. “Someone has to show them the way back.”

“Back where?”

He smiled, and for the first time Mara noticed that his teeth were tiny and sharp as shells.

“Anywhere but here.”

Behind her, the lighthouse began to turn.

One flash toward the village.

One toward the water.

One toward the moon.

And in the brief white instant between darknesses, Mara saw hundreds of faces beneath the sea, looking up.
